danish.title: Fjortende bog (1812) — Kapitel 17
paragraphs: Den russiske og den franske hærs bevægelser under felttoget fra Moskva tilbage til Njemen lignede en omgang russisk blindebuk, hvor to spillere er bundet for øjnene, og den ene af og til ringer med en lille klokke for at meddele fangeren, hvor han er. Først ringer han frygtløst med sin klokke, men når han kommer i knibe, løber han så stille væk som muligt, og tror ofte, at han flygter, mens han løber lige ind i sin modstanders arme.

I begyndelsen, mens de stadig bevægede sig langs Kalugavejen, gjorde Napoleons hære deres tilstedeværelse kendt, men senere, da de nåede Smolenskvejen, løb de med klokkens knebel holdt fast — og troede ofte, de flygtede, mens de løb lige ind i russerne.

På grund af den hurtige franske flugt og den russiske forfølgelse og den deraf følgende udmattelse af hestene var det vigtigste middel til nogenlunde at fastslå fjendens position — kavalerets rekognoscering — ikke tilgængeligt. Desuden kunne den information, der blev indhentet, som følge af de hyppige og hurtige positionsskift fra begge hære, ikke leveres i tide. Hvis man en dag fik meddelelse om, at fjenden dagen forinden havde befundet sig på en bestemt position, var den hær allerede to dagsmarcher længere fremme og i en helt anden stilling, inden der kunne foretages noget på den tredje dag.

Den ene hær flygtede, og den anden forfulgte. Hinsides Smolensk lå der flere forskellige veje åbne for franskmændene, og man skulle tro, at de i løbet af deres fire dages ophold kunne have erfaret, hvor fjenden var, kunne have lagt en mere fordelagtig plan og iværksat noget nyt. Men efter fire dages rast begyndte massen, uden manøvrer eller planer, igen at løbe ad det opkørte spor, hverken til højre eller venstre, men ad den gamle — den værste — vej, gennem Krasnoje og Orsja.

Da franskmændene ventede fjenden bagfra og ikke forfra, skiltes de i deres flugt og spredte sig over en strækning svarende til fireogtyve timers march. Forrest flygtede kejseren, så kongerne, så hertugerne. Den russiske hær, der ventede, at Napoleon ville tage vejen til højre hinsides Dnepr — hvilket var det eneste fornuftige at gøre — drejede selv til højre og kom ud på landevejen ved Krasnoje. Og her, som i et spil blindebuk, løb franskmændene ind i vores fortrop. Da de uventet så fjenden, faldt franskmændene i forvirring og standsede brat af pludselig skræk, men genoptog derefter deres flugt og opgav de kammerater, der var længere bagude. I tre dage løb separate dele af den franske hær — først Murats (vicekongens), så Davouts, derefter Neys — så at sige spidsrod for den russiske hær. De svigtede hinanden, opgav al deres tunge bagage, deres artilleri og halvdelen af deres mænd, og flygtede, idet de slap forbi russerne om natten ved at gøre halvbuer til højre.

Ney, som kom sidst, havde travlt med at sprænge Smolensks mure i luften, selvom de ikke generede nogen, for trods — eller på grund af — franskmændenes ulykkelige tilstand ønskede de at straffe det gulv, de havde slået sig på. Ney, der havde haft et korps på ti tusind mand, nåede Napoleon i Orsja med kun tusind mand tilbage, efter at have opgivet alle de øvrige og alle sine kanoner og at have krydset Dnepr om natten i hemmelighed ved et skovdækket sted.

Fra Orsja flygtede de videre ad vejen til Vilna, stadig spillende blindebuk med den forfølgende hær. Ved Berezina blev de igen bragt i uorden, mange druknede og mange overgav sig, men de, der kom over floden, flygtede videre. Deres øverste chef iførte sig en pelsfrakke, og efter at have sat sig i en slæde galopperede han alene af sted og efterlod sine ledsagere. De andre, der kunne, kørte også væk og overlod dem, der ikke kunne, til at overgive sig eller dø.

english.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: The movements of the Russian and French armies during the retreat from Moscow to the Niemen were like a game of Russian blindman's buff, where two blindfolded players stumble about and one occasionally rings a little bell to let the catcher know where he is. At first, the one with the bell rings it fearlessly, but when he gets cornered, he runs away as quietly as he can—and often, thinking he's escaping, runs straight into his opponent's arms.

At first, while still on the Kaluga road, Napoleon's armies made their presence known. But once they reached the Smolensk road, they ran with the bell's clapper held tight—and often, thinking they were escaping, ran right into the Russians.

Because of the speed of the French flight and the Russian pursuit, and the resulting exhaustion of the horses, the main means of determining the enemy's position—cavalry scouting—was unavailable. Besides, the frequent and rapid changes of position by both armies meant that even information received couldn't be delivered in time. If news came one day that the enemy had been at a certain position the day before, by the third day when anything could have been done, that army was already two days' march farther on and in a completely different spot.

One army fled and the other pursued. Beyond Smolensk there were several different roads available to the French, and one would have thought that during their four-day halt there they might have learned where the enemy was, devised a better plan, and tried something new. But after a four-day rest, the mob—with no strategy or plans—simply started running again along the beaten track, neither turning right nor left but taking the old, worst road through Krasnoe and Orsha.

Expecting the enemy from behind rather than ahead, the French spread out over a distance of twenty-four hours' march. At the very front fled the Emperor, then the kings, then the dukes. The Russian army, expecting Napoleon to take the road to the right beyond the Dnieper—which was the only sensible thing for him to do—turned right themselves and came out on the highway at Krasnoe. And here, as in a game of blindman's buff, the French ran into the Russian vanguard. Spotting their enemy unexpectedly, the French fell into confusion and froze with sudden fright, then resumed their flight, abandoning comrades who were farther behind. For three days, separate portions of the French army—first Murat's (the Viceroy's), then Davout's, then Ney's—ran the gauntlet of the Russian army. They abandoned one another, abandoned all their heavy baggage, artillery, and half their men, fleeing past the Russians at night by making wide detours to the right.

Ney, who came last, had been busy blowing up the walls of Smolensk, which were in nobody's way—because despite their desperate plight, or perhaps because of it, the French wanted to punish the floor they had stumbled on. Ney, who had started with a corps of ten thousand men, reached Napoleon at Orsha with only a thousand left, having abandoned all the rest along with his cannon, and having crossed the Dnieper by stealth at night at a wooded spot.

From Orsha they fled farther along the road to Vilna, still playing blindman's buff with the pursuing army. At the Berezina they fell into disarray again—many drowned, many surrendered—but those who got across the river fled on. Their supreme commander put on a fur coat and, climbing into a sleigh, galloped off alone, abandoning his companions. The others who could manage it drove away too, leaving those who could not to surrender or die.
